title: The Bank of America Merrill Lynch Art Conservation Project
description: An introduction to Bank of America Merrill Lynch's support of the conservation of three Tudor portraits.  Introduction by Kerry Miles (Bank of America Merrill Lynch), Sandy Nairne (Director, National Portrait Gallery).  The three portraits go on display as part of The Real Tudors: Kings and Queens Rediscovered at the National Portrait Gallery, London, from 12 September 2014 to 1 March 2015.   Find out more about the conservation project, supported by Bank of America Merrill Lynch: http://ow.ly/xSer8

asr.full_text: This program was created in partnership with American Art and Culture, under the guidelines of the British Institute for Contemporary and Contemporary Art, with the funding and funding from the American Arts Foundation in 2018. The Bank of America Merrill Lynch Arts Conservation Project is a unique program that provides funding for the conservation of works of art around the world that have a cultural significance or are important to the history of art. The objective of the program is really to foster and promote the heritage and the culture of the countries and regions where we live and work. Having worked with Bank of America Merrill Lynch on the Great Exhibition on Lucy and Freud's portraits a few years ago, we were delighted that the Bank has now made it possible to help us through their conservation program, and for us to therefore be able to undertake this rather particular program of conservation on some of the Tudor portraits. This came out of work we'd done with technical analysis of a few of these portraits. But this takes it a whole stage further of actually bringing these portraits into the best possible condition so that they can be seen with others in comparison and enjoyed by the widest possible public. This was an exciting opportunity for Bank of America to understand why and how some of the portraits of some of our most well known kings and queens were made. During that conservation many interesting techniques and findings came about, helping us to deepen our understanding about why these portraits were made. In the case of the portraits of Elizabeth I, there are many you can see it in comparison with the great portrait known as the pelican portrait that otherwise lives and belongs to the National Museums of Liverpool. So doing the conservation programme has allowed us to make comparisons, to understand both the similarities and the differences, and again for the works to be seen in quite a new way. I think every school child in Britain looks at these images and they're some of the iconic images of the monarchs and we just thought how important it was to conserve these for future generations, and really we just feel privileged to be involved in sort of the discovery that goes on behind, finding out why these portraits are made.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because its primary purpose is to document and explain Bank of America Merrill Lynch’s support for conserving historically significant Tudor portraits. Interviews with identified institutional representatives and footage of conservation work, including a before-and-after presentation of a treated portrait, reinforce the documentary and cultural-heritage context. The described material contains no observed request for payment, credentials, investment participation, or other audience action.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The main subject is art conservation and historical portraits, illustrated by a discussion of conservation findings and images labeled before and after treatment.
